description: A high-quality rapid TTS voice cloning model that reaches speeds of 150x realtime.

summary.one_liner: LuxTTS is a lightweight, ZipVoice-based text-to-speech model for voice cloning from a short reference clip, generating 48kHz speech at reported speeds above 150x realtime.
summary.what_it_does: The repository provides Python code to load the LuxTTS model (from the YatharthS/LuxTTS Hugging Face repo) on CUDA, CPU, or MPS devices. Users encode a reference audio file (WAV or MP3) into a voice prompt with encode_prompt, then call generate_speech on text to produce cloned speech. Sampling parameters include num_steps, t_shift, speed, rms loudness, return_smooth, and reference duration. Output is a 48kHz waveform that can be saved with soundfile. The README says it is distilled to 4 sampling steps and uses a custom 48kHz Vocos-based vocoder instead of ZipVoice's default 24kHz one. It also lists community projects such as a Gradio app, a ComfyUI node set, and an ONNX version.
use_cases: clone a voice from a short audio sample
generate speech from text in a cloned voice
fast local text-to-speech on a consumer GPU
batch narration or voiceover generation at 48kHz
integrate voice cloning into ComfyUI workflows
how_to_run: git clone <repository URL> (the README leaves the URL blank)
from zipvoice.luxvoice import LuxTTS; lux_tts = LuxTTS('YatharthS/LuxTTS', device='cuda')
notable: Outputs 48kHz speech, whereas many TTS models are limited to 24kHz
Distilled to 4 sampling steps from ZipVoice, with a modified sampling technique
Runs in about 1GB VRAM on local GPUs
Supports CUDA, CPU (with thread count), and Apple MPS devices
Community ports for Gradio, ComfyUI, and ONNX
caveats: Reference audio should be at least 3 seconds long for voice cloning
Currently runs in float32; float16 inference code is listed as a roadmap item, not yet released
Speed claims (150x realtime) are stated by the author for a single GPU, with CPU described as faster than realtime
keywords: make audio from text in someone's voice
